We will continue to focus on technology development with a forward-looking approach in a rapidly changing environment and aim to strengthen our position as a leading player in the global semiconductor market in the AI era.”

AMD Google Cloud Competition Sharpens as Helios Challenges Nvidia
AMD has launched its first complete rack-scale AI platform, turning the AMD Google conversation into a direct contest over who controls data center architecture.
The Helios system combines 72 Instinct MI455X accelerators, 18 EPYC processors, Pensando networking, and AMD’s ROCm software environment. AMD presented the production design at its Advancing AI event on July 23, 2026.
That launch changes AMD’s position in the market. It is no longer offering hyperscalers a collection of components that customers must assemble around another company’s networking and software. Helios gives AMD a coordinated rack that competes with Nvidia’s NVL72 systems and the vertically integrated infrastructure behind Google’s tensor processing units.
The headline specifications are substantial. A Helios rack carries approximately 31 terabytes of HBM4, or fourth-generation high-bandwidth memory, across its accelerators. AMD lists 2.9 exaflops of peak FP4 compute, a low-precision format commonly used for AI inference.
However, those figures do not settle the competition. Nvidia still has the stronger developer environment, a larger installed base, and an established rack-scale deployment model. Google controls its own models, cloud platform, networking, and custom TPU roadmap.
AMD’s reversal is more specific. The company has progressed from selling an alternative accelerator to proposing an alternative data center design. Customers now have to decide whether an open, multi-vendor rack can outweigh the operational advantages of a tightly controlled platform.
AMD Google Cloud Competition Is Moving Beyond Individual Chips
The Helios launch makes the complete rack, rather than the individual accelerator, AMD’s primary unit of competition.
Modern AI clusters cannot achieve useful performance by placing fast GPUs in conventional servers. Hundreds or thousands of accelerators must exchange model parameters, activations, and cached data with consistently low latency.
Rack-scale architecture treats an entire cabinet as one coordinated computing system. Compute trays, host processors, memory, cooling, power distribution, switches, and software are designed together.
AMD’s Helios platform uses 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs connected through UALink over Ethernet. UALink is an industry-backed interconnect intended to provide high-speed communication among accelerators from multiple vendors.
Each MI455X includes 432 GB of HBM4 and up to 23.3 terabytes per second of memory bandwidth, according to AMD’s published specifications. HBM places stacked memory close to the processor, reducing the delay associated with moving model data.
The rack also includes 18 EPYC “Venice” CPUs and Pensando Vulcano network interfaces. Its external scale-out networking uses Ultra Ethernet, an open specification designed for large AI and high-performance computing clusters.
Those details matter because data movement increasingly determines usable AI performance. A processor can advertise enormous peak throughput while spending part of its operating time waiting for memory or another accelerator.
Larger memory pools also allow systems to retain more model weights and key-value cache data near the processors. A key-value cache stores information generated during inference so the model does not recompute the entire conversation for every token.
That capability becomes important for long prompts, coding agents, research systems, and models that generate several alternatives before returning an answer. These workloads can consume memory rapidly even when the underlying model remains unchanged.
The AMD Google comparison therefore covers more than GPU performance. Google’s TPU systems use custom accelerators, proprietary interconnects, and software optimized for Google’s cloud and model development environment.
Google can tune those layers together because it controls them. AMD instead argues that customers can gain comparable system coordination while retaining choices among server manufacturers, networking suppliers, cloud platforms, and software frameworks.
Google Cloud has not announced Helios as a core accelerator platform. Its 2026 infrastructure roadmap emphasizes Google TPUs, Nvidia systems, and general-purpose virtual machines using AMD and Intel CPUs.
That distinction should remain clear. Google participates in AMD’s broader infrastructure environment, but Helios is not currently the foundation of Google Cloud’s AI accelerator strategy.
The relevant pressure comes from customer expectations. If AMD proves that open rack-scale systems can operate efficiently, buyers may demand similar flexibility from every cloud provider.
For developers searching for AMD Helios explained, the simplest answer is that AMD has built the cabinet, network, processors, and software into one deployable design. The harder question is whether operators can achieve its promised performance outside carefully selected demonstrations.
Helios Turns AMD Into a Systems Competitor
AMD’s most important change is organizational: the company now has to deliver a complete operating system for AI infrastructure, not merely competitive silicon.
AMD built its data center position largely through EPYC server processors. Its Instinct accelerators later gave cloud providers a second source for AI compute, particularly when demand exceeded available Nvidia capacity.
Helios moves the company farther up the stack. AMD must coordinate processor design, accelerator packaging, networking, firmware, compilers, libraries, cluster management, cooling, and serviceability.
That model resembles the approach Nvidia used with DGX and its NVL rack systems. Nvidia transformed from a chip supplier into a data center platform company by combining GPUs with NVLink, networking, CUDA libraries, reference systems, and deployment guidance.
AMD is pursuing the same outcome through different governance. It promotes ROCm as an open software environment and bases Helios on Open Compute Project hardware specifications.
The Open Compute Project publishes data center designs that manufacturers and operators can adapt. This approach can reduce dependence on one supplier, although “open” does not automatically mean interchangeable or easy to operate.
AMD also uses networking standards supported by other chip and equipment companies. That gives original equipment manufacturers room to incorporate merchant switches and their own management tools.
The practical benefit is negotiating leverage. A cloud provider can adopt AMD accelerators without surrendering every surrounding layer to AMD.
The corresponding burden is integration. When a proprietary system fails, the platform owner has clearer responsibility for diagnosing the problem. An open system can distribute that responsibility among the accelerator vendor, switch supplier, server manufacturer, software team, and cloud operator.
AMD is addressing that concern with customer commitments that extend beyond trials. Meta agreed to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct capacity across several hardware generations.
Shipments supporting Meta’s first gigawatt were scheduled to begin during the second half of 2026. The initial deployment uses a customized MI450-family accelerator, Venice CPUs, Helios architecture, and ROCm software, according to the Meta deployment.
Anthropic has separately committed to deploy up to 2 gigawatts of MI450-series GPUs in Helios systems. Its first gigawatt is scheduled to begin deployment during the first half of 2027.
That Anthropic agreement is especially meaningful because Anthropic trains and serves frontier models. Its workloads should expose weaknesses in memory management, collective communication, compiler behavior, and large-cluster reliability.
Microsoft has also said it will deploy Helios through Azure. Cerebras plans to place Helios systems in its data centers and combine them with its wafer-scale inference technology.
These commitments answer one question surrounding AMD Helios explained coverage. Helios is not merely a reference diagram waiting for a customer. Several large operators have attached deployment plans to it.
They do not answer whether those installations will reach their intended schedules, utilization rates, or economics. Gigawatt commitments describe potential infrastructure scale, not delivered computing capacity.
Building a large AI cluster requires electrical service, cooling equipment, construction, networking, memory supply, and working software. A delayed component can prevent a nominally available accelerator from producing billable tokens.
AMD has consequently entered a more demanding business. Its success will depend on complete cluster delivery and workload performance, not the shipment of individual chips.
AMD vs Nvidia AI Is Now a Rack-Level Fight
Nvidia remains the primary opponent because Helios directly attacks the company’s strongest advantage: control over the complete accelerated-computing stack.
Nvidia’s advantage begins with CUDA, its programming platform for GPU computing. CUDA includes compilers, libraries, debugging tools, and optimized kernels that developers have used for years.
The resulting software base creates switching costs. A model written in a common framework may technically run on different accelerators, yet its custom operations and deployment tools can still depend on Nvidia software.
ROCm supports major AI frameworks and has improved across successive releases. AMD has also published migration tools and optimized libraries for training, inference, communication, and model serving.
Software parity remains workload-specific. A standard benchmark can run well while an internal production model encounters unsupported operations, unstable kernels, or slower compilation.
That is why the AMD vs Nvidia AI debate cannot be settled through one peak-performance figure. Buyers need measurements covering model accuracy, token throughput, latency, power consumption, operator time, and cluster availability.
Helios appears competitive in several physical dimensions. Its 72 MI455X accelerators provide approximately 31 TB of HBM4, which gives the rack a large local memory pool.
AMD claims the MI455X delivers 40.3 petaflops of peak FP4 performance per device. Multiplying that figure across 72 accelerators produces the advertised 2.9 exaflops for Helios.
Nvidia has published a higher rack-level FP4 figure for its 72-GPU Vera Rubin NVL72 configuration. Independent examination of the claims found that AMD’s per-GPU advantage did not translate into a higher rack total under the vendors’ published measurements.
That rack comparison illustrates a recurring benchmarking problem. Vendors can choose device-level or system-level denominators, different numerical formats, and favorable workload assumptions.
Peak theoretical operations also exclude communication stalls and software overhead. A system with lower nominal compute can finish a model run sooner if its software and network keep more processors occupied.
Nvidia’s advantage is therefore broader than raw throughput. Its systems arrive with a known deployment pattern, experienced operators, and extensive support across commercial AI software.
AMD’s counterargument centers on memory, standards, and customer control. Helios gives buyers an integrated system without making every interface dependent on one proprietary supplier.
That is a credible difference, but it is not a free advantage. Open standards often require several vendors to make compatible products on synchronized schedules.
Nvidia can change a processor, link, switch, and software library as part of one roadmap. AMD must coordinate UALink, Ultra Ethernet, server manufacturers, switch vendors, memory suppliers, and cloud operators.
The AMD vs Nvidia AI contest will be decided partly through execution discipline. AMD needs its partners to turn specifications into repeatable installations, while Nvidia must show that its integrated approach justifies tighter platform control.
Google adds another competitive route. Its TPU infrastructure does not attempt to create a merchant GPU platform that every cloud can deploy. Google builds custom systems primarily for its own cloud services and internal AI workloads.
This gives Google an unusually direct feedback loop among model researchers, compiler teams, chip designers, and data center engineers. It can optimize hardware around the workload patterns it expects to serve.
However, customers choosing TPUs accept a closer relationship with Google Cloud. Moving the same workload elsewhere may require different hardware assumptions, software tuning, and operational practices.
The AMD Google question is thus not simply which processor is faster. It asks whether buyers prefer a cloud-specific vertical stack or portable infrastructure assembled around open interfaces.
Nvidia occupies a third position. It sells a highly integrated platform across multiple clouds, making CUDA portable among providers while keeping the accelerator environment closely tied to Nvidia.
AMD has to break that three-way problem. It must offer enough integration to operate like Nvidia, enough openness to differentiate from Nvidia, and enough cloud availability to compete with Google’s infrastructure reach.
The Specifications Still Need Production Proof
Helios is AMD’s strongest data center design to date, but most of its decisive claims remain engineering projections rather than sustained production results.
AMD’s product pages describe the MI455X using peak theoretical throughput and internal engineering estimates. Those figures provide a useful upper bound, but customers rarely operate large models at that limit.
A production system encounters power restrictions, network congestion, failed components, checkpointing, software updates, and uneven request patterns. These factors determine how much purchased compute becomes useful work.
Helios also relies on direct liquid cooling. Liquid cooling removes heat more efficiently than conventional air systems, but it requires compatible facilities, distribution units, monitoring, and maintenance procedures.
Many large operators already use liquid cooling for high-density AI clusters. Enterprises with conventional server rooms may face more extensive infrastructure changes.
Serviceability presents another test. The Helios design divides 72 accelerators across repeatable four-GPU trays, which should allow technicians to replace components without rebuilding an entire rack.
Actual repair time depends on failure isolation and spare-part availability. Operators need telemetry that can identify whether a slowdown originates in a GPU, cable, switch, firmware layer, or collective communication library.
Memory supply adds uncertainty. Each Helios rack contains 31 TB of HBM4, and hyperscale commitments imply demand for large quantities of advanced memory and packaging.
AMD depends on external manufacturing and memory partners. A strong accelerator design cannot meet deployment targets if packaging yields or HBM shipments constrain completed systems.
The company’s major customer agreements also include forward-looking timelines. Meta’s first deployment begins in the second half of 2026, while Anthropic’s starts during the first half of 2027.
Those schedules leave limited public production evidence today. Customers should distinguish between announced capacity, installed capacity, accepted systems, and accelerators serving real traffic.
Benchmark disclosure will be equally important. AMD has participated in MLPerf, an industry benchmark suite that measures training and inference under defined conditions.
Future MI455X results should include server configurations, software versions, power settings, accuracy targets, and availability classes. Comparable submissions matter more than isolated company charts.
Even standardized benchmarks cannot reproduce every production workload. Long-context inference, sparse mixture-of-experts models, reinforcement learning, and agentic systems create different communication and memory patterns.
A mixture-of-experts model activates selected groups of parameters for each input rather than using every parameter. This can reduce compute requirements while increasing routing and communication complexity.
AMD previously projected large gains for MI400-family systems on these models. Buyers should treat those gains as workload-dependent until independent testing reproduces them.
ROCm represents the other central uncertainty. Software maturity cannot be summarized by the number of supported frameworks because enterprises often maintain custom kernels and internal deployment systems.
Migration costs include code changes, validation, monitoring updates, staff training, and parallel capacity during the transition. A lower hardware cost can disappear if engineering teams spend months repairing production pipelines.
Developers evaluating AMD Helios explained material should therefore inspect the software bill of materials, not only the accelerator specification. They need supported framework versions, kernel coverage, communication libraries, observability tools, and escalation procedures.
Google and Nvidia both benefit from mature operational loops. Google tunes its infrastructure against internal services, while Nvidia receives feedback from a large base of developers and cloud partners.
AMD now has the customers needed to build a similar loop. Meta, Microsoft, Anthropic, Oracle, and Cerebras represent distinct workloads that can reveal different platform weaknesses.
The strongest signal will not be another partnership announcement. It will be evidence that these customers expanded deployments after operating the first systems.
That distinction keeps the analysis grounded. Helios establishes that AMD can design a serious rack-scale competitor. It does not yet establish that the company can deliver and support those racks at comparable production efficiency.
What the AMD Google Contest Will Reveal Next
Three near-term signals will determine whether Helios becomes a durable platform or remains a useful second source for selected customers.
The first signal is the initial production ramp during the second half of 2026. AMD and its partners need to ship complete systems, install them in prepared facilities, and move customer workloads beyond testing.
Volume matters, but acceptance matters more. A rack sitting in a staging environment does not validate performance, reliability, or operational readiness.
Evidence of Meta and Microsoft running sustained production workloads would strengthen AMD’s argument. Delays between hardware delivery and useful deployment would expose integration or facility constraints.
Investors and buyers should watch AMD’s reporting language carefully. References to product shipments, customer acceptance, revenue recognition, installed capacity, and active workloads describe different stages.
The second signal is independently comparable MI455X performance. Public results should test both training and inference across several model types.
Useful comparisons will report throughput, latency, energy consumption, and memory behavior at the system level. Per-device claims should not substitute for a 72-accelerator rack measurement.
This signal can strengthen or weaken the AMD vs Nvidia AI case quickly. Competitive workload results would show that Helios translates its memory and interconnect design into usable performance.
A wide gap between peak claims and measured output would reinforce Nvidia’s software and integration advantage. Inconsistent results across frameworks would point toward ROCm optimization gaps.
The third signal is repeat purchasing. Meta, Anthropic, Microsoft, and other early customers have already provided substantial demand commitments.
A second deployment phase would indicate that the platform met operational and economic targets. A quiet reduction in planned capacity would carry the opposite meaning.
Google Cloud’s response also deserves attention. Google does not need to adopt Helios to affect AMD’s prospects.
It can expand TPU availability, improve compatibility with common AI frameworks, or offer more flexible access to Nvidia and other processors. Those moves would make Google Cloud a stronger answer for customers seeking alternatives without managing rack infrastructure.
Conversely, broader Google support for AMD accelerators would increase cloud portability and reduce the risk of committing to ROCm. No such Helios deployment should be assumed until the companies announce it.
The AMD Google contest therefore exposes a larger shift in infrastructure buying. Customers are no longer comparing isolated accelerator specifications. They are choosing among governance models for compute.
Google offers a vertically integrated cloud and custom accelerator path. Nvidia provides an integrated merchant platform available through numerous clouds and system vendors. AMD proposes an open rack architecture that partners can adapt.
Each model exchanges one form of control for another. Vertical integration can simplify optimization while increasing platform dependence. Open interfaces can preserve choice while increasing coordination costs.
For developers, the immediate implication is practical. Hardware diversity will make portability, profiling, and workload-specific benchmarking more valuable.
Teams should separate model logic from vendor-specific kernels when feasible. They should also preserve reproducible evaluation sets so migrations can be measured against accuracy and service-level requirements.
Infrastructure buyers should request production evidence at the full cluster level. Processor benchmarks cannot reveal network oversubscription, cooling limits, recovery behavior, or operator effort.
They should also identify which party owns a system-level problem. An open architecture only helps when support contracts and diagnostic responsibilities remain clear.
Knowledge workers will experience this competition indirectly. More infrastructure choices can expand model availability and reduce dependence on a single capacity provider.
However, the result will not automatically be lower latency or wider access. Providers must translate hardware capacity into reliable services, and applications must use that capacity efficiently.
Tracking the expanding stream of specifications, benchmark qualifications, and deployment announcements can become difficult. A searchable technical knowledge base can help engineering teams preserve the evidence behind infrastructure decisions.
Helios has already changed the competitive frame. AMD can now present a coherent rack against Nvidia’s rack systems and Google’s vertically integrated AI infrastructure.
The next phase is less theatrical. Customers must install the equipment, migrate software, run models, repair failures, and decide whether to order more.
That is the test readers should follow. Watch accepted production capacity, comparable system benchmarks, and repeat deployments. Together, those signals will show whether AMD has created another accelerator option or a lasting alternative data center platform.
As the AMD Google competition develops, ask a simple question whenever a new claim appears: does it describe a specification, a shipment, or a production workload? The distinction will reveal who is actually gaining ground.

Did the authors of the Energy Department’s controversial 2025 climate report confuse two layers of the Earth’s atmosphere, and then use faulty analysis to question evidence of anthropogenic climate change? That is the extraordinary suggestion in a recent paper by five climate scientists published in the journal Earth’s Future.
Earlier this year, at a panel discussion about the Energy Department report, one of the authors exhibited a previously unpublished figure. It showed a dramatic discrepancy between predicted and observed temperatures in the tropical lower stratosphere—the second layer of the Earth’s atmosphere—and was used to support the claim that “models fail in the upper atmosphere.”
Benjamin Santer, the lead author of the Earth’s Future article, said the figure was wrong, and appeared to show observations from the troposphere, the lowest layer of the Earth’s atmosphere, instead of the stratosphere.
Santer and his Earth’s Future coauthors say this echoed a similar, and similarly inaccurate, argument in the Energy Department report, which they thought may have been based on this flawed analysis. They warn that until the Energy Department report is corrected or retracted it “will continue to misinform policymakers and the public about the reality of human effects on climate.”
The Bulletin contacted all five of the Climate Working Group members who wrote the 2025 report. Ross McKitrick, a Canadian economist, said the mistake in the unpublished chart stemmed from a coding error. John Christy, a climate scientist at the University of Alabama, said the figure was not relied on for the Climate Working Group report.
When asked if they had any plans to correct, clarify, or respond to this paper, or to any of the other errors and misrepresentations that other scientists have identified in the 2025 report, McKitrick said that the group has been disbanded and barred from publishing a revised version of the document or any other response to their critics.
The unrevised and uncorrected report is still circulating and can be used to propose or set policy in the United States.
He says the Climate Working Group members are caught between a rock and a hard place: Their report was thoroughly dissected and criticized by dozens of scientists, and while they say they have addressed those concerns in a revised version, they also contend they are unable to publish without violating a court order that ruled the group’s work illegal. As a result of a lawsuit filed by environmental advocacy groups, a judge found that the Energy Department and the Climate Working Group violated the law by not adhering to transparency rules and ordered the release of roughly 100,000 pages of emails and other documents related to the group’s work.
“Blame the people who brought the lawsuit against the DOE for the lack of response to date,” Judith Curry, a climate scientist and professor emerita at the Georgia Institute of Technology, told the Bulletin in an email.
The other Climate Working Group members—Steven Koonin, who presented the unpublished chart, and Roy Spencer—did not respond to requests for comment. The Energy Department also did not respond when contacted by the Bulletin for comment.
The continuing controversy over the report highlights the ongoing conflict between climate scientists who say their research is being misrepresented, and the Trump administration, which tried to draw on its own hand-picked set of skeptics to justify rolling back environmental regulations. Meanwhile, the unrevised and uncorrected report is still circulating and can be used to propose or set policy in the United States.
The Climate Working Group saga began in the spring of 2025, when Energy Secretary Chris Wright asked four scientists and one economist, all widely recognized as climate contrarians, to write a report that “critically review[s] the current state of climate science.” Emails released as part of the lawsuit appear to show that the group sought to provide scientific justification for the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of the endangerment finding—the legal basis for regulating greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act. The endangerment finding asserted that rising atmospheric concentrations of six greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide and methane, pose a risk to public health and future generations.
In April 2025, Roy Spencer, a meteorologist and climate scientist at the University of Alabama, advised his colleagues not to get too “mired in the technical details” at the expense of explaining how it will impact “eventual policy decisions related to the Endangerment Finding.” A few days later, he added, “About all I can hope is that what we write will provide sufficient ‘reasonable scientific doubt’…to call into question the original reasoning for the EPA Administrator’s decision that CO2 presents a threat to human health and welfare.”
Their report, “A Critical Review of Impacts of Greenhouse Gas Emissions on the U.S. Climate,” was published on July 29. The EPA issued its proposal to rescind the endangerment finding, which extensively cited an early version of the Climate Working Group report, on the same day.
In August, the Environmental Defense Fund and the Union of Concerned Scientists sued the Trump administration for tasking what it described as a secretive and one-sided group of experts with writing a report to inform federal policymaking, which it said was a violation of the Federal Advisory Committee Act.
In early September, more than 85 climate experts published a critical review of the Energy Department report, citing dozens of examples of cherry-picking, selective citation, and scientific misrepresentation.
Ironically, the Climate Working Group likely foresaw many of these criticisms in advance. As emails between members of the group reveal, during the editing process, Steven Koonin, a physicist and former chief scientist at BP and undersecretary for science in Obama’s Energy Department, now a fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution, asked Microsoft Copilot to review the draft for scientific accuracy and potential bias. The AI tool flagged numerous issues including “selective emphasis,” “outdated or narrow sourcing,” “selective citation,” “cherry-picked” evidence, “interpretive bias,” and “interpretive overreach.” To this critique, climatologist Judith Curry responded, “This is amazing, far better than what we would get from ‘real’ scientists.” At other points, the authors seemed frustrated that the LLMs they queried seemed to give greater weight to papers and voices representing the climate consensus than climate contrarians.
Around the same time, Secretary Wright informed the Climate Working Group that their services were no longer needed. The Trump administration then argued in court that the environmental groups’ lawsuit was moot because the Climate Working Group had been dissolved—an argument US district court judge William Young did not buy. In January 2026, he determined the Energy Department had violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act.
In February, the EPA officially repealed the endangerment finding, although notably without relying on the beleaguered Climate Working Group report.
So why are climate scientists still focused on a year-old report that has already been extensively criticized?
The main reason, given at the top of the Earth’s Future article, is that this report continues to inform policymakers and the public about the causes and consequences of anthropogenic climate change.
Although the judge found the Climate Working Group violated the law, he stopped short of ordering the Energy Department to strike their report from the federal record, as the environmental groups suing the administration had asked. That means that, although EPA chose to sidestep “scientific controversies” entirely, the agency could have cited it as evidence in its final repeal of the endangerment finding. Earlier this year, a group of Republican attorneys general did cite the report when demanding the Federal Judicial Center strike the chapter on climate science from a scientific reference manual for judges. So did Florida’s “Department of Government Efficiency,” which railed against cities and counties “squandering millions in virtue-signaling about a so-called climate crisis” in a report that cites the Energy Department climate report extensively.
The second reason is more personal. The Climate Working Group cast doubt on decades of research into and evidence of human-caused climate change, while citing work by Santer and others to support their conclusions. But Santer says the paper referenced provides “some of the most compelling scientific evidence to date of a human fingerprint on atmospheric temperature.”
“Imagine how it feels to have your life’s work incorrectly dismissed in an official government report—a report issued by the same agency you spent 30 years working for,” Santer told the Bulletin. “It does not feel good.”

— Benjamin Santer, retired Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory atmospheric scientist
To fully understand the “human fingerprint,” issue in question—in other words, evidence of anthropogenic climate change—requires an abbreviated climate science history lesson.
In 1967, Syukuro Manabe and Richard Wetherald published what has been described as “arguably the greatest climate-science paper of all time.” Using a pioneering climate model, the scientists not only estimated how much warming would occur if atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were doubled—they also predicted that rising carbon dioxide levels would warm the troposphere (the lowest layer of the Earth’s atmosphere) while cooling the stratosphere (the layer above the troposphere). The reason this happens is essentially because of the greenhouse effect: carbon dioxide prevents heat radiated out from the Earth from escaping into space, warming the Earth’s surface, while simultaneously emitting more radiation back into space, cooling the stratosphere.
Manabe and Wetherald’s paper laid the groundwork for the field of climate fingerprinting, which seeks to attribute changes in the Earth’s climate to either human or natural causes. Subsequent decades of research—more advanced modeling as well as observations (measurements from weather balloons and satellites)—have generally confirmed Manabe and Wetherald’s predictions over 50 years ago, and scientists like Santer have confidently attributed these trends to human activity, specifically carbon dioxide emissions from burning fossil fuels.
However, in the section of the Energy Department report on “stratospheric cooling,” the Climate Working Group dismissed decades of research. “A combination of tropospheric warming and stratospheric cooling is a commonly cited ‘fingerprint’ of anthropogenic climate change,” the group wrote. “Stratospheric warming since 2000 coincides with continued surface and tropospheric warming, a pattern that is not found in climate model simulations and is not apparently consistent with the anthropogenic fingerprint.”
Santer and other climate scientists say this statement is wrong for several reasons. As they wrote in their rebuttal last year, the middle and upper stratosphere has been cooling since 1979 (when satellite measurements first became available) to the present day; the lower stratosphere cooled from 1979 to 2000 and then saw “muted trends” (neither strong warming nor cooling) since 2000.
But there’s also a simple explanation for why the lower stratosphere has stopped cooling or even begun to warm slightly since 2000: ozone. Like carbon dioxide, ozone is a greenhouse gas, meaning it traps heat radiating out from the Earth’s surface, but also absorbs heat from the sun. The widespread use of chlorofluorocarbons in aerosol sprays, refrigerants, solvents, and other applications depleted the amount of ozone in the atmosphere in the latter half of the 20th century, sparking global fears of increased cancer risk (ozone blocks many of the sun’s harmful ultraviolet rays), as well as cooling the stratosphere. When those chemicals were phased out as a result of the Montreal Protocol, the ozone layer stabilized in the 1990s and began recovering in the early aughts. More ozone meant that the lower stratosphere stopped cooling as quickly, and maybe even warmed slightly.
In their report, the Climate Working Group authors quote from a 2018 paper that found the lower stratosphere began warming in the 21st century, but as Santer and others have pointed out, they omit the part of the sentence that explains this is consistent with ozone recovery.
The authors then conflate this warming in the lower stratosphere with warming across the entire stratosphere and used that to suggest that climate models are wrong and to question evidence of anthropogenic climate change.
At least one internal reviewer, prepublication, also pointed out that this section of the report was misleading, cherry picks data, and takes it out of context. “This section should be removed or amended to note that stratospheric temperatures are influenced by multiple factors and that a comprehensive analysis of stratospheric temprature [sic] trends is fully consistent with those projected under climate warming scenarios,” they wrote.
The Climate Working Group made minor tweaks to the text in response to this and other queries, but did not address the substance of this critique when they had the opportunity.
“To the extent we were unclear about the distinction between the lower stratosphere and the upper (or entire) stratosphere it is a fair criticism and our revision goes into detail about the differences,” McKitrick wrote in emailed comments to the Bulletin.
Even though the Climate Working Group has been officially dissolved, the members have continued to discuss and promote their report. At a February event organized by the Civitas Institute at the University of Texas, John Christy, Steven Koonin, and Ross McKitrick presented their findings on extreme weather, climate models, and how climate change could impact economic growth. Andrew Dessler, a climate scientist at Texas A&M who co-led the scientific rebuttal to their report last year (and is a coauthor on the Earth’s Future paper), responded to each of their presentations.
When it was Koonin’s turn to discuss climate models, he doubled down on the claim that “Models fail in the upper atmosphere.” To illustrate this point, he exhibited a chart that showed a rough bell curve of climate models that almost all predicted cooling in the tropical lower stratosphere between 2000 – 2025, and then a bright red line far outside the mean model prediction, which was supposed to represent the actual observations. As the caption explained, “About ¾ of the models…predict continued cooling, whereas observations clearly show warming.”
The authors of the Earth’s Future paper inferred that this chart may have been the basis for the Climate Working Group’s claim that the stratosphere has warmed since 2000, contrary to what models predicted.
The only problem is that the chart has no basis in reality, according to critics. As Santer and his coauthors write in the Earth’s Future paper, they were unable to replicate the observations from the figure Koonin showed. Although they can’t be sure where those observations came from, they wrote that they “appear to be from the troposphere rather than the lower stratosphere.” If that were true, it would be an extraordinary and embarrassing mix-up.
John Christy later confirmed to Dessler that the observations in Koonin’s figure were incorrect, according to the authors of the Earth’s Future paper, but did not clarify how the mistake happened. In an email to the Bulletin, McKitrick said the mistake was due to a coding error and shared a corrected version of the unpublished chart—which still shows observations that are slightly warmer than model predictions, but nowhere near as drastic a difference as the original.
Both McKitrick and Christy expressed outrage that neither the authors nor the publisher of the Earth’s Future article gave them the opportunity to respond to criticism. Both also reiterated that what was published in July 2025 was what they describe as a draft report, although nothing in the press release, the energy.gov page where the report is linked, or the report itself indicates that it is merely a draft. In fact, the preface says that they submitted a draft for internal review in May, and they thank “a team of anonymous DOE and national lab reviewers whose input helped improve the final report.”
McKitrick and Christy say that they’ve gone over all of the comments in the rebuttal led by Dessler and Robert Kopp and have prepared a response and revised report, but are unable to publish anything.
“Unfortunately our group was disbanded due to the FACA lawsuit and we were forbidden from publishing a revised version or even our response material: we are still under that constraint and the problem remains unresolved,” McKitrick wrote.
While the working group has ceased to exist, there does not appear to be any prohibition on individual members from discussing or publishing on the issue either individually or collectively. In the September letter dissolving the group, Secretary Wright thanked them for challenging climate orthodoxies and starting a “much-needed debate in this area,” concluding: “Each of you remains free, as always, to continue engaging in that debate.”
Shortly after, Curry told E&E News that the members of the group would continue working outside the government to revise their report.
But McKitrick said that the Energy Department has since told them that they “cannot publish something as the ‘Climate Working Group’ or under any group name that might suggest to the court that we are still functioning as that same entity.”
McKitrick called it “a scientific disservice” when journals publish an “ambush attack” without allowing the other side to respond in print. “People end up talking past each other and you only get one side of the story, which doesn’t advance knowledge,” he said.
For his part, Santer said he would welcome a response to the Earth’s Future paper. Santer also reiterated that the problem is not just that the Climate Working Group made mistakes, but that they have failed to correct those mistakes.
“If, as a scientist, you get things wrong in an official government report—or in a presentation, in an open public presentation that’s up on YouTube—you can either set the record straight or not,” he said. “They’ve chosen not to set the record straight.”
